parsed.hook: Great Southern’s cool maritime climate and ancient lateritic soils give this Pinot Noir a savory edge—think wild thyme and ironstone dust over bright cherry. At a decade old, it’s a rare snapshot of how Western Australia’s southern coast can age gracefully without oak overload.
parsed.wine_summary: Plantagenet’s Omrah Pinot Noir is the workhorse of Great Southern, a region that punches above its weight in Australia’s cool-climate conversation. The 2011 comes from vineyards in Mount Barker and Frankland River, two of the five sub-regions that define Great Southern’s diversity. Mount Barker’s elevation (up to 400m) and lateritic gravels—iron-rich, free-draining soils formed from weathered granite—give the wine its taut acidity and herbal lift. Frankland River’s warmer sites contribute darker fruit and a touch of spice, but the maritime influence (proximity to the Southern Ocean) keeps ripeness in check. Plantagenet, founded in 1968, was one of the first to prove this region could grow Pinot Noir with structure, not just fruit. The Omrah line is their entry-level, but it’s built to reflect place, not just price point.
parsed.terroir_expression: Great Southern’s lateritic soils—especially the gravelly sandy loams derived from granite and gneiss—are the backbone of this wine’s character. These soils force vines to dig deep, stressing them just enough to concentrate flavors while retaining acidity. The maritime climate, with its cool summers (average January temps of 19°C) and high rainfall (900mm annually), slows ripening, preserving the grape’s natural brightness. The result is a Pinot Noir that tastes like the place: red cherry and pomegranate underpinned by wet stone and a whisper of wild rosemary. The 2011 vintage, a cooler year with a late harvest, amplified these traits, giving the wine a leaner, more savory profile than warmer years.
parsed.vinification_summary: Plantagenet ferments this Pinot Noir in stainless steel to preserve fruit purity, then ages it in a mix of older French oak barriques (typically 10-20% new) for 9-12 months. The oak is subtle—just enough to round out the tannins without adding vanilla or toast. Cold soaking (pre-fermentation maceration at 10-12°C for 3-5 days) extracts color and aroma without harsh tannins, a technique that works well with Great Southern’s naturally high acidity. The wine is bottled unfiltered, which can leave a slight sediment over time but also preserves texture. The 2011’s bronze medal at TEXSOM suggests it was a solid, if not flashy, vintage—typical of the Omrah line’s reliability over showiness.
